A.explanation: A systematic error such as a zero error can be reduced by recalibrating or adjusting the apparatus.

B.explanation: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount, while scatter between repeats is the feature of random error.

C.explanation: Random errors can involve the observer such as reaction time, but also environmental fluctuations and instrument noise, so not always the person.

D.explanation: Random deviations are sometimes high and sometimes low, so their mean tends toward the true value when several measurements are averaged.

hints: Notice the question contrasts repeat readings: one error type scatters results above and below, the other shifts them consistently.
Recall that a zero error or uncalibrated apparatus adds the same offset each time, while random effects vary unpredictably.
Think about what averaging does to values scattered on both sides of the true value versus values that all share the same shift.
walkthrough: Identify the two definitions: a systematic error is a consistent bias in one direction, for example a ruler with a worn zero, and a random error is unpredictable scatter, for example variation in stopwatch reaction time.
A systematic error repeats in the same way, so adjusting, re-zeroing or calibrating the apparatus directly reduces it.
A random error gives a different reading each time, and it is not always caused by the person because supply fluctuation or vibration can also cause scatter.
Averaging several repeats allows positive and negative random deviations to partly cancel, giving a mean closer to the true value, but it does not remove a constant systematic shift.
Only the statement about reducing random errors by taking the average of several measurements matches this physics. This is option D.
